reasons: The cross-origin rule allows all origins together with credentials.
Benchmark figures are hardcoded and not sourced.
Only 12 of 28 sections were available, so the rest is unexplained here.
It is unclear whether this is the active backend or an older copy.

terms.meaning: a browser rule about which websites may call this server.
a folder of files served as they are, such as images or pages.
a typical figure for an industry.
a class that looks at inputs and writes reasoning and advice.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Setup, cross-origin rules and exporter
sections.what: Loads the web tools and data libraries, sets cross-origin rules, creates the static folder, and creates the Excel exporter when the app starts.
sections.why: Likely reason: standard setup for a web app. The exporter is made once and reused.
sections.watch_out: Allowing every origin with credentials lets any website use a visitor's session with this server.

sections.name: CompanyInfo
sections.title: Company information shape
sections.what: Holds the company name, model name, industry, start year and number of periods.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Industry is free text, so spelling must match the benchmark table to get specific advice.

sections.name: RevenueAssumptions
sections.title: Revenue assumptions shape
sections.what: Holds starting revenue and a list of yearly growth rates.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The growth list length is not checked against the number of periods.

sections.name: CostStructure
sections.title: Cost structure shape
sections.what: Holds yearly percentage lists for cost of goods, research, and selling and admin costs.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Values are assumed to be fractions such as 0.2 rather than 20, and nothing checks this.

sections.name: CapExAssumptions
sections.title: Capital spending shape
sections.what: Holds yearly capital spending and the number of years over which it is depreciated.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The depreciation years are not checked to be positive.

sections.name: WorkingCapital
sections.title: Working capital shape
sections.what: Holds the number of days for receivables, inventory and payables.
sections.why: Likely reason: these are the standard inputs for cash tied up in day-to-day operations.
sections.watch_out: Day counts are not checked for sensible ranges.

sections.name: Financing
sections.title: Financing shape
sections.what: Holds starting debt, interest rate and tax rate.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Rates are assumed to be fractions, and nothing checks this.

sections.name: ValuationInputs
sections.title: Valuation inputs shape
sections.what: Holds the beta and terminal growth rate used to value the company.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Terminal growth must be below the discount rate for valuation to make sense, which this shape does not check.

sections.name: FinancialModelRequest
sections.title: Full model request shape
sections.what: Combines all the inputs above into one request for a full model, with a flag for using AI research.
sections.why: Likely reason: one request carries everything the model needs.
sections.watch_out: The AI research flag is accepted, but this part of the file does not show what it changes.

sections.name: AgentResponse
sections.title: Agent reply shape
sections.what: The standard reply from an agent: its name, reasoning text, a list of recommendations, and optional data.
sections.why: Likely reason: every agent returns the same shape so the interface can show them the same way.
sections.watch_out: Recommendations must be a list of text, or replies will fail.

sections.name: IndustryResearchAgent (part 1)
sections.title: Built-in industry benchmark table
sections.what: Holds fixed benchmark figures for five industries, such as typical beta, margins and cost ranges.
sections.why: Likely reason: built-in starting values so the app works without web research.
sections.watch_out: The figures have no stated source, and they are the only data this agent uses.

sections.name: IndustryResearchAgent: analyze
sections.title: Industry comparison and advice
sections.what: Compares the user's cost and growth inputs with the industry figures, then writes reasoning text and recommendations.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives plain-language feedback on whether the user's assumptions fit the industry.
sections.watch_out: Missing inputs fall back to made-up default percentages, so the comparison can use numbers the user never entered.

sections.name: FinancialAnalysisAgent (part 1)
sections.title: Financial analysis: growth and margin checks
sections.what: Works out how fast revenue grew, how profitable the company is each year, and how much cash it generated. It writes a plain-English summary and a short list of advice lines that the app shows as the financial agent's opinion.
sections.why: Likely reason: turns raw numbers into readable findings so the user does not need to read every table. Reason for the early exit when there is no data is not stated beyond the message itself.
sections.watch_out: The revenue growth figure divides by one less than the number of years, so a model with only one year will fail with a divide-by-zero error.

sections.name: FinancialAnalysisAgent (part 2)
sections.title: Financial analysis: cash flow and margin advice
sections.what: Adds advice lines about whether cash flow is positive, whether growth is very high, and whether profit margins are improving. These lines join the recommendations returned to the screen.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives a quick verdict on risk. The thresholds, such as 10 percent for margins and 40 percent for growth, are written into the code with no stated source.
sections.watch_out: The thresholds are fixed numbers in the code, not user settings, so changing what counts as healthy means editing this file.

sections.name: ValuationAgent (part 1)
sections.title: Valuation check: where the value comes from
sections.what: Splits the enterprise value into the part from the forecast years and the part from the long-term estimate after the forecast. It also reports the cost of capital (WACC) and terminal growth, and warns when the result depends heavily on long-term guesses.
sections.why: Likely reason: a large share of value far in the future makes the answer fragile, so the code flags it. Reason not stated otherwise.
sections.watch_out: The warning levels (75 percent, 60 percent, 3 percent growth, 8 percent and 15 percent WACC) are fixed numbers, so they may not suit every industry.

sections.name: ValuationAgent (part 2)
sections.title: Valuation check: value range and output
sections.what: Creates a rough low and high enterprise value by scaling the result about 10 percent up and down, then returns the valuation advice and summary numbers.
sections.why: Likely reason: a quick range helps the user see uncertainty in the answer. The 10 percent is a rough scaling, not a full recalculation at a different cost of capital.
sections.watch_out: The range is labelled as a change in WACC of 10 percent, but it is really a 10 percent scaling of the whole value, so the label can mislead.

sections.name: read_root
sections.title: Home page route
sections.what: When someone opens the app's main address, the server sends the web page from the static folder. If that page is missing, it sends a short message saying the frontend was not found.
sections.why: Likely reason: serves the user interface from the same server, so only one program needs to run.
sections.watch_out: The page location is built from where this file sits, so moving the file or the static folder will quietly show the fallback message instead of the page.

sections.name: health_check
sections.title: Health check route
sections.what: Returns a simple healthy status and version 1.0.0 so that tools can confirm the server is running.
sections.why: Likely reason: a standard way for monitoring tools and Docker to check that a service is alive.
sections.watch_out: It does not test the database, the Excel tool, or the language model server, so a healthy result does not prove the analysis will work. The version number is typed in by hand.

sections.name: get_industries
sections.title: List of supported industries
sections.what: Returns the six industry names the app accepts: SaaS, Software, E-commerce, Manufacturing, Healthcare and Retail. The screen can use this list to offer choices.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Likely reason: keeps the choices fixed so the research step recognises each one.
sections.watch_out: The list is typed in here and must match what the industry research step understands. The code does not check this match.

sections.name: research_industry
sections.title: Industry research endpoint
sections.what: Takes the company details and inputs, runs the industry research step, and returns its benchmarks and advice to the caller.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the screen ask for industry benchmarks separately from building the full model.
sections.watch_out: Because the inputs are a second part of the request body, a caller that sends only the company details will receive an error.

sections.name: analyze_model (part 1)
sections.title: Full model: build statements and cost of capital
sections.what: When the screen asks for a full model, it builds revenue, costs, capital spending, working capital and the three financial statements. It then works out the cost of capital (WACC) using market data.
sections.why: Likely reason: the screen needs the whole model in one call. The order of steps matters because later figures depend on earlier ones.
sections.watch_out: The debt share is set to a fixed 20 percent when there is no debt. Otherwise it divides debt by debt plus base revenue, which is an unusual measure, so check it before relying on the WACC.

sections.name: analyze_model (part 2)
sections.title: Full model: valuation and agent results
sections.what: Calculates the discounted cash flow value, runs the three advisory agents, converts the statement tables into plain lists, and returns everything in one result.
sections.why: Likely reason: the screen shows the values, the cost of capital and the advice together. The code does not state why tables are converted to lists, but web responses need plain data.
sections.watch_out: If any single step fails, the whole analysis fails with one error message, and the user cannot see which step caused it.

sections.name: analyze_model (part 3)
sections.title: Full model: error handling
sections.what: If anything in the full model fails, the server returns an error with code 500 and the error text.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the screen show a failure instead of the server crashing.
sections.watch_out: The raw error text is sent to the user, which can reveal internal details about the code.

sections.name: export_to_excel (part 1)
sections.title: Excel export: rebuild the model
sections.what: Rebuilds the same model used by the analysis route, so the Excel file matches what the user saw. It creates the revenue, cost, capital, statement and cost of capital figures.
sections.why: Likely reason: each export recalculates from the inputs rather than storing an earlier result. The code does not say why the steps are copied rather than shared.
sections.watch_out: The same model-building steps appear in two places, so a change made in one route can be missed in the other.

sections.name: export_to_excel (part 2)
sections.title: Excel export: collect inputs and save file
sections.what: Gathers the user's inputs into one list, passes them with the statements and valuation to the Excel tool, and returns the file name and a download link.
sections.why: Likely reason: the Excel tool needs every assumption in one place so it can write the assumptions sheet.
sections.watch_out: The inputs list does not include the model name or the revenue growth key that the Excel tool reads, so this export is likely to fail as the code stands. The growth rates are sent under a different name.

sections.name: export_to_excel (part 3)
sections.title: Excel export: error handling
sections.what: On failure, prints the full error trace to the server console and returns an error with code 500 to the screen.
sections.why: Likely reason: the trace gives the developer the exact line that failed, which the short screen message does not show.
sections.watch_out: The trace only goes to the server console, so someone who is not watching that console will not see the cause.

sections.name: download_file
sections.title: Download an exported file
sections.what: Sends a previously exported Excel file to the browser by its file name, or returns a not found error if the file is missing.
sections.why: Likely reason: the export step only returns a name, so this route is what lets the user actually get the file.
sections.watch_out: The file name comes straight from the web address and is joined to the exports folder with no check for unusual names, so treat this route as open to anyone who can reach the server.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Starting the server
sections.what: When this file is run directly, it prints the local addresses and starts the server on port 8000, listening on all network addresses and restarting when code changes.
sections.why: Likely reason: the reload setting is for development, so code changes show up without a manual restart. Reason for listening on all addresses is not stated.
sections.watch_out: Listening on all addresses makes the server reachable from other machines on the network. The reload setting is meant for development, not for a live service.

summary: A single-file web backend for the financial modeling tool with request shapes, a rule-based industry benchmark agent, and Excel export routes. Only the first 12 of 28 sections were available to review, so the rest of the file is not explained here.
purpose: Serve the interface with endpoints for research, analysis and Excel files.
why: Reason not stated in the code. It may be a standalone version that sits beside the structured backend folder.
how: Loads the web tools and an Excel exporter, sets permissive cross-origin rules, creates a static folder, defines request shapes, then defines an industry agent with fixed benchmarks that compares inputs with them. Later routes are not reviewed here.
inputs: Company, industry and financial inputs in requests, and the benchmark table written in the code.
outputs: Analysis text, recommendations and benchmark data, plus Excel files from routes not reviewed here.
risks: Cross-origin rules allow any website to call the server with credentials. Benchmark numbers are fixed in code with no source. Unknown industries silently use the Software numbers.
debug: If industry figures look wrong, check the benchmark table in the agent. If a page cannot reach the server, check the cross-origin settings. The static folder is created at startup.
